claims.text: A machine-learning-enhanced atomistic simulation can predict temperature-dependent electrical conductivity in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly incorporating point-defect and 1 wt.% oxygen scattering will improve prediction accuracy relative to perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed accuracy advantage will apply in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The modeled bulk HfNbTaTiZr has an intrinsic population of point defects.
The modeled specimen contains a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
Defects, including oxygen interstitials, modify local bonding in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defects, including oxygen interstitials, modify the local electronic structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
The defect-induced local changes produce additional electron-scattering events.
Additional defect and impurity scattering influences charge transport.
The simulation will statistically sample defect configurations and their effects on electron scattering.
Sampling defect configurations will capture the interplay between thermal activation and impurity/defect scattering.
Traditional perfect-crystal analytical models neglect impurity and defect scattering.
The simulated conductivity will align closely with experimental measurements across both specified temperature ranges.
The proposed simulation will have lower relative errors than idealized defect-free models.
A potential acceptable prediction-error threshold is less than 20% relative to experiment.
Conventional pristine-crystal predictions typically show larger discrepancies from experiment because they omit defect and oxygen-impurity scattering.
The approach is applicable only to HfNbTaTiZr with similar defect populations and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The predictions may not transfer to purer, more highly oxidized, or otherwise compositionally different samples, or outside the stated temperature windows.
Conductivity measurements near 150 K and 800 K are proposed as benchmarks for the simulation.
A relative prediction error greater than 20% at either benchmark is declared to falsify the hypothesis.
